Intersect the missing digits in each cell’s row, column, and box; repeatedly fill single candidates, branching on a cell with the fewest remaining candidates if necessary. The completed grid is:

3 2 9 7 4 1 5 6 8
8 5 4 6 3 2 1 9 7
4 9 6 3 1 7 2 8 5
5 1 8 2 9 4 7 3 6

questions.prompt: The sets x₁,…,x₁₀₀ and y₁,…,y₁₅₀ have mean zero and equal standard deviations. Which ratio is Σxᵢ²:Σyᵢ² closest to?
hints: For zero mean, variance is the sum of squares divided by sample size (or size minus one).
Equal variances make the sums proportional to their denominators.
questions.solution: With population standard deviations, σ²=Σxᵢ²/100=Σyᵢ²/150, so the ratio is 100:150=2:3. With sample standard deviations the ratio is 99:149≈0.6644, still closest to 2:3≈0.6667 rather than 1,0.8165,or0.4444. This assumes the common standard deviation is nonzero; if both data sets are identically zero, the displayed ratio is undefined.
questions.theory: The arithmetic mean of n observations is their sum divided by n. The median is a middle order statistic after the data are sorted: for odd n it is observation (n+1)/2, while for even n it is the average of the two central observations. The mode is a value attaining the greatest frequency and need not equal either the mean or median. Population variance is the mean squared deviation from the mean; sample variance uses denominator n-1 instead. When the mean is zero the squared deviations are simply the squares of the observations. Extreme observations affect the mean strongly but may leave the median unchanged. State the variance convention and avoid reading a statistic directly from unsorted data.  Equality of nonzero standard deviations permits equating the corresponding sums of squares after dividing by the appropriate degrees of freedom. Zero standard deviation implies every observation equals its mean and produces the undefined ratio zero to zero, so the usual ratio calculation requires nondegeneracy.

similar_questions.solution: The sums are nσ², namely 20·4=80 and 30·4=120; ratio 2:3.

similar_questions.prompt: A zero-mean sample of size 11 has sample variance 9. Find its sum of squares.
similar_questions.solution: Sample variance uses denominator n−1=10. Therefore Σxᵢ²=10·9=90.

questions.prompt: Two cylindrical candles have unequal heights and diameters. The shorter lasts 13 hours and the longer 9 hours. Lit together, their heights are equal after 5 hours. Find the ratio of original heights (shorter:longer).

questions.solution: Assuming uniform burning of each cylindrical candle, heights decrease linearly. If original heights are s,l, the remaining heights after 5 hours are s(1−5/13)=8s/13 and l(1−5/9)=4l/9. Equality gives 8s/13=4l/9, hence s/l=13/18. questions.theory: The arithmetic mean of n observations is their sum divided by n. The median is a middle order statistic after the data are sorted: for odd n it is observation (n+1)/2, while for even n it is the average of the two central observations. The mode is a value attaining the greatest frequency and need not equal either the mean or median. Population variance is the mean squared deviation from the mean; sample variance uses denominator n-1 instead. When the mean is zero the squared deviations are simply the squares of the observations. Extreme observations affect the mean strongly but may leave the median unchanged. State the variance convention and avoid reading a statistic directly from unsorted data.

similar_questions.solution: Sum=15 and n=5, so mean=3. The middle value and most frequent value are both 3; all three statistics coincide.

questions.prompt: Let X be a nonempty finite set and Y={f⁻¹(0): f is a real-valued function on X}. Which statement is true?

options.C: There is a bijection from X to Y
options.D: There is a surjection from X to Y

hints: A zero set is a subset of X.
Can every subset be realized by a function taking only the values 0 and 1?
questions.solution: Every zero set is a subset of X. Conversely, for each subset S⊆X define f(x)=0 on S and f(x)=1 off S; then f⁻¹(0)=S. Thus Y is exactly the power set of X and has 2ⁿ members, n=|X|. It is finite, and 2ⁿ>n for n≥1, excluding both a bijection and a surjection from X.
questions.theory: Finite counting rests on injective assignments, partitions, and careful tracking of possible configurations. The pigeonhole principle states that if N objects are assigned to k boxes, some box has at least ceil(N/k) objects. This conclusion guarantees existence of one crowded box, not the same occupancy in every box. The power set of an n-element set has 2ⁿ elements, since each element has two independent choices, inclusion or exclusion. An injection from a finite set to another requires the target to be at least as large; a surjection requires the domain to be at least as large. To prove a counting claim, identify the objects and boxes or construct a bijection. Counterexamples should satisfy all hypotheses and show that the stronger proposed conclusion fails.  The preimage of zero is a set, not an inverse function. Distinct functions may have the same preimage. Counting possible zero sets therefore requires identifying the family of subsets they realize rather than counting the infinitely many functions themselves.

similar_questions.prompt: Find all zero sets of real functions on {a,b}.
similar_questions.solution: They are ∅,{a},{b},{a,b}, realized by 0/1 functions. There are 2²=4.

similar_questions.prompt: Can a 3-element set map surjectively to its power set?
similar_questions.solution: Its power set has 2³=8 elements, while an image of a 3-element domain has at most 3 elements. No.

questions.prompt: Consider (a) Σₙ₌₁∞ sin(nπ/2)/√n and (b) Σₙ₌₁∞ log(1+1/n²). Which is true?
hints: Write out the first few values of sin(nπ/2).
Use alternating-series convergence for (a) and log(1+t)≤t for (b).
questions.solution: The zero even terms leave (a)=1−1/√3+1/√5−1/√7+⋯. The positive magnitudes decrease to zero, so the alternating-series test proves convergence (not absolute convergence). For (b), 0≤log(1+1/n²)≤1/n² and Σ1/n² converges; comparison proves convergence. Therefore C is true.
questions.theory: Real analysis studies limits, continuity, differentiation, and convergence using precise quantifiers. A sequence converges to L if every positive tolerance eventually bounds its distance from L. Its limsup is the limit of the suprema of its tails; for a periodic sequence it is the largest recurring value. A numerical series converges when its partial sums have a finite limit. Comparison with a convergent nonnegative series, the alternating-series test, and Dirichlet’s test have distinct hypotheses that must be verified. A differentiable function is continuous, and an accumulation point of its zeros is itself a zero. Rolle’s theorem requires continuity on a closed interval and differentiability inside. Compactness supplies convergent subsequences of bounded real sequences. Be careful not to confuse conditional convergence with absolute convergence.

similar_questions.prompt: Does Σ(−1)ⁿ⁻¹/n converge absolutely?
similar_questions.solution: The magnitudes 1/n decrease to zero, so the alternating series converges. The absolute series is harmonic and diverges, so convergence is conditional.

similar_questions.prompt: Prove Σlog(1+1/n³) converges.
similar_questions.solution: For t≥0, log(1+t)≤t. Hence its terms lie between 0 and 1/n³, whose p-series converges. Comparison proves convergence.

questions.prompt: f:ℝ→ℝ is differentiable and f,f′ have no common zeros in [0,1]. Which is true?

options.B: f has at most finitely many zeros in [0,1]
options.C: f has infinitely many zeros in [0,1]

hints: An infinite subset of a compact interval has an accumulation point.
Use difference quotients along the zeros to show that the derivative also vanishes there.
questions.solution: If f had infinitely many distinct zeros in the compact interval, they would have a convergent subsequence xₖ→c∈[0,1]. Continuity gives f(c)=0. Since xₖ≠c, the difference quotients [f(xₖ)−f(c)]/(xₖ−c) vanish. Differentiability on ℝ, including at endpoints, gives f′(c)=0, a contradiction. Hence there are finitely many zeros. f(x)=x−1/3 refutes A and D; f=1 also refutes C and D.

Compactness supplies convergent subsequences of bounded real sequences. Be careful not to confuse conditional convergence with absolute convergence.  A zero is simple in the differentiable sense when its derivative is nonzero. An accumulation of distinct zeros forces a common zero of the function and derivative by continuity and the definition of derivative. Compactness turns an infinite set of zeros in a bounded closed interval into such an accumulation.

questions.prompt: f is a real cubic with exactly one real root, which is simple. Which statement holds for every antiderivative F?

options.A: F has exactly one real root
options.B: F has exactly four real roots
options.C: F has at most two real roots
options.D: F has at most one real root

hints: Relate distinct zeros of F to zeros of F′ using Rolle’s theorem.
Three zeros of F would force two distinct zeros of the cubic.
questions.solution: If F had three distinct real zeros, Rolle’s theorem on the two intervening intervals would give two distinct real zeros of F′=f, contradicting the hypothesis. Thus F has at most two distinct real roots. For f=x³+x, antiderivatives are x⁴/4+x²/2+C. C>0 gives no roots, excluding A and B; C<0 gives exactly two roots, excluding D. Hence C is the unique universal conclusion.

similar_questions.prompt: If f has at most two distinct real zeros, how many can an antiderivative have?
similar_questions.solution: Four zeros of an antiderivative would produce three zeros of f by Rolle. Therefore at most three distinct zeros are possible.

questions.prompt: Iₙ is the identity. Which is true?

options.A: Real A(3×2),B(2×3) with BA=I₂ necessarily have AB=I₃
options.B: A=[[3,3],[1,2]] has an integer-entry B with AB=I₂
options.C: A=[[3,1],[1,2]] over ℤ/6ℤ has a B with AB=I₂
options.D: Every nonzero real diagonal 3×3 matrix has a right inverse

hints: Distinguish rank constraints over ℝ from unit determinants over a ring.

questions.solution: A: rank(AB)≤2, so AB cannot be I₃. B: det A=3 and the unique real inverse is (1/3)[[2,−3],[−1,3]], not integral. C: the determinant is 6−1=5, a unit modulo 6 with inverse 5. questions.theory: A linear map is represented by a matrix once bases are chosen. Its rank is the dimension of its image and its nullity is the dimension of its kernel; the rank-nullity theorem says their sum equals the dimension of the domain. Products satisfy rank(AB)≤min(rank A,rank B). A square matrix over a field is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero. An eigenvector is a nonzero vector mapped to a scalar multiple of itself; the scalar is its eigenvalue. An invariant subspace is mapped into itself. Real symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis. Positive definiteness means xᵀAx>0 for every nonzero real x. Distinguish a nonzero matrix from a nonsingular matrix, and specify the coefficient field or ring when testing invertibility.

similar_questions.prompt: Does [[2,0],[0,1]] invert over ℤ/6ℤ?
similar_questions.solution: Its determinant 2 is not a unit modulo 6. Equivalently 2b≡1 has no solution, so no inverse exists.

Independent polynomial powers of the curved parameter force separate equality conditions for the corresponding data summaries.

similar_questions.prompt: For iid N(μ,σ²), find a minimal sufficient statistic.
similar_questions.solution: Expanding Σ(xᵢ−μ)² shows dependence through Σxᵢ and Σxᵢ². The likelihood-ratio criterion forces equality of both, so (Σx,Σx²) is minimal sufficient.

similar_questions.prompt: For Yᵢ=aᵢθ+εᵢ with known aᵢ and unknown σ, find a sufficient statistic.
similar_questions.solution: The residual sum is ΣYᵢ²−2θΣaᵢYᵢ+θ²Σaᵢ². Thus (ΣYᵢ²,ΣaᵢYᵢ) is sufficient, and the ratio criterion proves minimality when the design is nonzero.

questions.prompt: X₁,…,Xₙ,n≥2, have density θx^(θ−1),0<x<1,θ>0. Which is the UMVUE of 1/θ?
hints: Transform each observation by −log X.
The transformed sum is complete sufficient gamma, and its mean is n/θ.
questions.solution: Set Zᵢ=−log Xᵢ. Then P(Zᵢ>z)=P(Xᵢ<e⁻ᶻ)=e⁻θᶻ, so Zᵢ∼Exp(rate θ), with mean 1/θ. S=ΣZᵢ is gamma(shape n,rate θ) and complete sufficient for θ (a full one-parameter exponential family). Therefore S/n=−ΣlnXᵢ/n is unbiased for 1/θ and, by Lehmann–Scheffé, is its UMVUE. B and C estimate functions of θ rather than its reciprocal; D has mean 2/θ.
questions.theory: Statistical inference uses observations to estimate unknown parameters or test hypotheses. A sufficient statistic retains all likelihood information about the parameter; factorization proves sufficiency. Minimal sufficiency can be verified by the likelihood-ratio criterion: the ratio of two data likelihoods is parameter independent exactly when their statistic values agree. Completeness means every integrable function of the statistic with expectation zero at every parameter is almost surely zero. A complete sufficient statistic yields unique minimum-variance unbiased estimators by the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem. For testing, a monotone likelihood ratio gives one-sided uniformly most powerful rejection regions in the corresponding statistic. Bayesian squared-error estimation uses the posterior mean. Check distribution parametrization, tail-quantile conventions, and whether an estimator is unbiased for the requested parameter or its reciprocal.

similar_questions.solution: S=ΣX is complete sufficient gamma. S/n has expectation 1/θ and is a function of S, so is UMVUE.

similar_questions.prompt: For S∼Gamma(n,rate θ),n>1, find an unbiased estimator of θ.
similar_questions.solution: E[1/S]=θ/(n−1), so (n−1)/S is unbiased. If S is complete sufficient it is also UMVUE.

questions.prompt: A coin has head probability p, prior Beta(5,5). In 25 independent tosses there are 10 heads. Find the Bayes estimate under squared-error loss.
hints: Update the prior shape parameters by heads and tails separately.

questions.prompt: An OLS line from n=10 observations is ŷᵢ=1.5+0.8xᵢ. Corrected sums are Syy=5,Sxx=6. Find adjusted R² rounded to two decimals.
hints: Find fitted sum of squares using slope² times Sxx.
Adjust using residual df 8 and total df 9.
questions.solution: In simple OLS with intercept, SSR=b²Sxx=0.8²·6=3.84. Thus SSE=5−3.84=1.16 and R²=3.84/5=.768. There are n−2=8 residual degrees of freedom and n−1=9 total degrees of freedom. Adjusted R²=1−(1.16/8)/(5/9)=1−.261=.739, which rounds to .74. Option .77 is the ordinary R² rounded, not the adjusted value.
questions.theory: Ordinary least squares minimizes residual squared error. With an intercept, total corrected sum of squares decomposes into fitted and residual sums of squares. In simple regression the fitted sum of squares is slope² times the corrected x sum of squares; R² is fitted divided by total, and adjusted R² corrects residual and total sums using their degrees of freedom. For p-dimensional normal observations with covariance Σ, the centered scatter matrix has a Wishart distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom and scale Σ. Whitening transforms it to identity scale, and its trace is a sum of independent squared standard normals with (n−1)p degrees of freedom. Distinguish a scalar trace distribution from the matrix-valued Wishart law, and distinguish n from n−1 when the sample mean is estimated.

questions.prompt: A Latin square has error sum-of-squares degrees of freedom 42. Find treatment degrees of freedom.
hints: Use the standard Latin-square error df formula.
Solve (v−1)(v−2)=42, then subtract one for treatment df.
questions.solution: For order v, error df=(v−1)(v−2)=42. Thus v²−3v−40=0=(v−8)(v+5), giving admissible v=8. Treatment df=v−1=7. The negative root is not a possible design order.
questions.theory: An experimental design organizes treatment comparisons while controlling nuisance variation. A Latin square of order v has v rows, v columns, and v treatments, with every treatment occurring once in each row and each column. There are v² observations. Under the standard additive analysis of variance model, the corrected total degrees of freedom are v²−1. Rows, columns, and treatments each consume v−1 degrees of freedom, leaving (v−1)(v−2) for error. These formulae assume one observation per cell and the standard no-interaction model. A computed order must be an admissible positive integer, and the requested component’s degrees of freedom should be extracted only after finding that order. Do not confuse treatment degrees of freedom with the number of treatments.

questions.prompt: Maximize z=3x+4y subject to x+y≤12,2x+3y≤30,x+4y≤36,x,y≥0. Find the optimum.
hints: Seek a nonnegative combination of constraints equal to the objective.
Adding the first two left sides gives exactly 3x+4y.
questions.solution: Add the first two constraints: 3x+4y≤12+30=42. This is a global upper bound on the objective. The point (6,6) satisfies x+y=12,2x+3y=30,x+4y=30≤36 and nonnegativity, and has value 42. Thus it attains the bound and is optimal. Options B and C are feasible but have value 41. D violates 2x+3y≤30 because 8+24=32. Equality in both bound constraints uniquely gives (6,6).
questions.theory: Linear programming optimizes a linear objective over a set specified by linear equalities and inequalities. With nonnegative decision variables in two dimensions, feasible constraints form a convex polygon or an unbounded region. If a finite optimum exists on a nonempty polytope, at least one vertex achieves it. Candidate vertices come from intersections of boundary lines, including coordinate axes, but each must be checked against every inequality. A dual upper bound can prove optimality without enumerating all vertices: express the objective as a nonnegative combination of constraint left sides, then use their right sides. A feasible point attaining this bound is optimal. Comparing only the listed options is insufficient unless global optimality is also established.

similar_questions.solution: Adding the constraints gives objective≤13. Their intersection is y=3,x=2, feasible and attaining 13, so optimal.
